Aristotle quote sources

18 passages attributed to Aristotle in this archive, each with the locator that lets you find it in the work itself — and the one thing that most often goes wrong when people quote Aristotle.

Quote source / Aristotle

How to cite this author, and what circulates under the name that is not theirs to give.

Sourcing profile

Language of the works
Ancient Greek
Cited here from
The Nicomachean Ethics (I.1, I.7, II.1, II.6, VIII, IX), the Metaphysics (I.1, I.2), and the Politics (I.2).
How to cite it
Use the Bekker number — 1107a, 982b12 — not a page number. Bekker numbering was fixed in the nineteenth century and is printed in the margin of every scholarly edition and translation, so it is the one locator that survives a change of translator.
Where quotations of this author go wrong
The works we have are lecture notes and treatises rather than the dialogues Aristotle wrote for publication; the flowing prose is the editor's or the translator's, and the numbered arguments are the text. Quoting a polished English sentence and calling it “what Aristotle wrote” overstates how finished the surviving text is.

1 of the passages below have been worked through against the cited edition, with the original-language wording and the circulating variants recorded on their own pages.

Frequently asked questions

Where can I check quotations attributed to Aristotle?

Use the Bekker number — 1107a, 982b12 — not a page number. Bekker numbering was fixed in the nineteenth century and is printed in the margin of every scholarly edition and translation, so it is the one locator that survives a change of translator. This archive cites Aristotle from The Nicomachean Ethics (I.1, I.7, II.1, II.6, VIII, IX), the Metaphysics (I.1, I.2), and the Politics (I.2). Every passage listed on this page carries that locator, so it can be found in any edition of the work.

What is the most common mistake when quoting Aristotle?

The works we have are lecture notes and treatises rather than the dialogues Aristotle wrote for publication; the flowing prose is the editor's or the translator's, and the numbered arguments are the text. Quoting a polished English sentence and calling it “what Aristotle wrote” overstates how finished the surviving text is.

What language did Aristotle write in?

Ancient Greek. Any English sentence you read is a translation, so a complete source names the translator as well as the passage.
